{"id": "21:1/q29", "question": "What overarching theme does this opening establish for the sūra?", "turns_on": "Which of the sūra's connected themes is placed at its center.", "positions": [{"id": "21:1/q29/p1", "position": "The Hour, resurrection and universal judgment are certain and near.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī includes death as a route to the Hour and judgment of eminent and humble; the Creator has no partner to impede it. Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the sūra treats prophethood on monotheism and resurrection, emphasizing threat; Study Quran cites 54:1. Ibn Kathīr connects the warning with 16:1 and 54:1–2, where God's command and the Hour are near but disbelievers reject signs."}, {"id": "21:1/q29/p2", "position": "The core theme is God's oneness, transcendence and unified prophetic revelation.", "reasons": "Asad says the prophets repeatedly teach this truth, which people forget; the title reflects their recurrence and the flow supports one community."}, {"id": "21:1/q29/p3", "position": "The warning anticipates truth's triumph and Quraysh's defeat.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī says the sūra predicts the conquest of Mecca while giving embattled Muslims glad tidings and warning Quraysh."}]}
{"id": "21:1/q30", "question": "What divine attributes or spiritual states does the opening evoke?", "turns_on": "How the announced account is read as a present spiritual warning and encounter.", "positions": [{"id": "21:1/q30/p1", "position": "The divine names express justice, mercy, sovereignty, respite and decisive judgment.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī describes God as wise and just, Allah as unrivaled King, the All-Merciful as granting existence, and the Merciful as saving whom He wills afterward."}, {"id": "21:1/q30/p2", "position": "God's favor shelters the obedient and gives neglecters respite, while repentance is met with mercy and arrogance crushed.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī connects confession to remembrance, concealment of sin to divine favor, and return to mercy."}, {"id": "21:1/q30/p3", "position": "God enables outward striving and grants inner realization and witnessing.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī says striving brings future recompense while abiding witnessing grants immediate nearness; obedient and disobedient people receive reward and punishment respectively."}, {"id": "21:1/q30/p4", "position": "The minor resurrection can make accounting spiritually present now.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī says people who understood resurrection would already witness their own accounting."}]}
{"id": "21:1/q31", "question": "How do theologians classify closeness and forgetfulness?", "turns_on": "Whether forgetfulness is knowledge loss, a distinct meaning, or a condition of the heart.", "positions": [{"id": "21:1/q31/p1", "position": "Closeness is a created state, and forgetfulness is loss of needed knowledge.", "reasons": "Jishumī reports theologians classing proximity with combination, separation, motion and rest. Al-Qāḍī defines forgetfulness as loss of necessary ordinary knowledge."}, {"id": "21:1/q31/p2", "position": "Being or occurrence can be treated as a separate genus of state.", "reasons": "Jishumī reports this alternative classification among theologians."}, {"id": "21:1/q31/p3", "position": "Forgetfulness can be an independent entity or meaning.", "reasons": "Jishumī reports this view without further argument."}, {"id": "21:1/q31/p4", "position": "Forgetfulness can be corruption in the heart.", "reasons": "Jishumī records this as another account."}]}
{"id": "21:1/q32", "question": "What did the opening inspire in reported poetry or preaching?", "turns_on": "Which reported response gives poetic or homiletic expression to the warning.", "positions": [{"id": "21:1/q32/p1", "position": "It inspired a couplet on people heedless while death grinds on.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr relays Ibn ʿAsākir's report that Abū Nuwās praised Abū al-ʿAtāhiya's verse as drawn from this opening."}, {"id": "21:1/q32/p2", "position": "It accompanies preaching that the world is nearly spent.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī quotes a predecessor likening the remaining world to a little liquid in a vessel."}]}
{"id": "21:1/q33", "question": "What is the status of Qur'anic speech discussed with this passage?", "turns_on": "Whether 'speech' means recited conventional signs or a wider disclosure, and what can bear temporal predicates.", "positions": [{"id": "21:1/q33/p1", "position": "Recited speech is a conventional sign of meaning; its sound tokens arise in time, while the convention itself has no temporal status.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī says each reciter's sounds are distinct, and speech counts as one by shared intended meaning. Ordered eternal letters are impossible; conventional speech is neither a real act nor an essential attribute, although external sounds are acts. His analysis treats meaningful verses as neither eternal nor originated in themselves."}, {"id": "21:1/q33/p2", "position": "Speech can be understood more broadly as whatever reveals hidden reality.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī says effects disclose latent perfection and essential attributes disclose essence; philosophers call God's knowledge, power, life and world His speech. Divine knowledge is eternal, created signs originated, and revelation originated as imparted but eternal as known. He rejects multiplying divine attributes from such reductions."}, {"id": "21:1/q33/p3", "position": "The dispute over an eternal or created recited Qur'an is unproductive.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī says eternal sounds are impossible and divine knowledge needs no additional Qur'an attribute; multiplying every reduced attribute would produce limitless attributes. Scripture's plain use concerns recited speech."}]}
{"id": "21:1/q34", "question": "What variant writing or recitation issue is reported nearby?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "21:1/q34/p1", "position": "A wāw may be dropped in connected recitation and then omitted in writing.", "reasons": "Al-Lawāmiḥ says avoiding two sukūns accounts for the spelling, comparing 42:24; al-Ālūsī cites a poetic line where ḍamma betrays the missing wāw, although some grammarians consider the omission poetic necessity."}]}
{"id": "21:26/q01", "question": "Who made the claim that the Merciful took a child?", "turns_on": "Whether the reported occasion identifies a particular Arab group or Jewish claimants, and whether the verse's scope extends beyond its occasion.", "positions": [{"id": "21:26/q01/p1", "position": "Khuzāʿa made the claim, sometimes specified as a group of that tribe.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī, al-Jishumī, al-Baghawī, al-Kashshāf, al-Rāzī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī, al-Biqāʿī, al-Bursawī, al-Ālūsī, Ibn ʿĀshūr, and Study Quran report Khuzāʿa as the occasion. Al-Qurṭubī and Study Quran add that they worshipped angels hoping for intercession; al-Rāzī and Ibn ʿĀshūr add a marriage to jinn, and al-Bursawī specifies leading jinn. Ibn ʿĀshūr locates them on Mecca’s outskirts; al-Ālūsī calls this the famous account."}, {"id": "21:26/q01/p2", "position": "Quraysh or other Arab polytheists made the claim, with al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith named in one report.", "reasons": "Muqātil names Meccan unbelievers including al-Naḍr. Ibn al-Jawzī reports Ibn ʿAbbās naming Quraysh and Ibn Isḥāq naming al-Naḍr. Al-Wāḥidī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Ālūsī, Ibn ʿĀshūr, Asad, Kuran Yolu, and Study Quran mention Quraysh, Arabs, or pagans; Ibn ʿĀshūr cites 16:57, Study Quran 37:149–153 and 43:16–17, and Kuran Yolu 16:57, 17:40, 43:15–20."}, {"id": "21:26/q01/p3", "position": "Jews made the claim, saying God intermarried with jinn and angels descended from that union.", "reasons": "Qatāda is reported by Yaḥyā ibn Sallām, ʿAbd al-Razzāq, Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Durr, and al-Ālūsī; al-Qurṭubī notes Maʿmar’s recension also says 'some groups.' Al-Biqāʿī reports Jews as another antecedent. Al-Rāzī links the jinn claim to 37:158, though in his account Khuzāʿa says it."}, {"id": "21:26/q01/p4", "position": "The wording also encompasses Christians who call Jesus God's son and Jews who call Ezra His son.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the verse refutes all these claims; al-Jishumī mentions Christians and other unbelievers; al-Ālūsī says every attribution of offspring is condemned. Abu Ḥayyān and Kuran Yolu mention the Christian and Jewish claims; Study Quran gives Christian sonship as an alternative and cites 4:171."}]}
{"id": "21:26/q02", "question": "What does اتَّخَذَ mean and how is it formed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "21:26/q02/p1", "position": "It means taking or making something one's own; here it can suggest treating someone as a child.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī reads the verb as pretending or behaving as one with a child. Al-Rāghib, quoted by al-Bursawī, defines akhdh as placing or acquiring something, by taking or force, and notes figurative usage for fever or a captive. He derives ittakhadha from akhdh in the iftiʿāl form; it takes two objects and functions like jaʿala."}]}
{"id": "21:26/q03", "question": "Why is God called ٱلرَّحْمَٰنُ here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "21:26/q03/p1", "position": "The title recalls that all beings depend on His beneficence, making the offspring claim absurd.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says every existent receives its existence from the Merciful's beneficence. Al-Ālūsī says the title presents everything besides Him as His dependent creature and heightens the absurdity of a child."}]}
{"id": "21:26/q04", "question": "Whom does the alleged وَلَدًا refer to?", "turns_on": "Whether the phrase is read by its reported occasion about angels or by the wider range of claims it rebukes.", "positions": [{"id": "21:26/q04/p1", "position": "The alleged offspring are angels, called God's daughters.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās as reported by al-Wāḥidī, and al-Ṭabrisī, explicitly identify the child as angels. Muqātil, Qatāda's reports, Ibn Isḥāq, al-Wāḥidī, Ibn al-Jawzī, and later accounts connect this with Arabs' or Jews' claim; Ibn ʿĀshūr cites 16:57 and Study

Quran 37:149–153, 43:16–17."}, {"id": "21:26/q04/p2", "position": "The alleged offspring may include Jesus and Ezra as well as angels.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya says Christians called Jesus God's son and Jews called Ezra His son; Abu Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī likewise extend the scope. Asad includes prophets such as Jesus and angels; Kuran Yolu mentions Jesus and angels. Study Quran gives Jesus' divine sonship as an alternative referent, citing 4:171."}]}
{"id": "21:26/q05", "question": "What is the number and gender range of وَلَدًا?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "21:26/q05/p1", "position": "Walad can denote one or many, sons or daughters; here the claim concerns daughters.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī says it can be singular, plural, or collective like māl. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it a collective with the same form for singular and plural, including sons and daughters, and cites 16:57 for the daughters in view."}]}
{"id": "21:26/q06", "question": "Why is divine offspring impossible, and what kind of fatherhood is excluded?", "turns_on": "Whether 'father' means biological or adoptive filiation, or a restricted metaphor of special relation.", "positions": [{"id": "21:26/q06/p1", "position": "Literal offspring or adoption cannot apply to God.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī and al-Ṭabrisī distinguish begetting, which entails bodily nature, from adoption, which substitutes a non-child for a child; when true filiation is impossible, its adoptive analogy fails. They distinguish this from possible special divine affection or friendship. Al-Jishumī adds that Christian eternal hypostases cannot form a son or make three one. Al-Rāzī argues resemblance and difference entail composition and contingency. Al-Biqāʿī argues a child shares a nature with its parent. Ibn ʿĀshūr and Kuran Yolu say children imply need or deficiency; Ibn ʿĀshūr cites 10:68. Asad cites 19:92 for God's remoteness from that imperfection. Al-Kashshāf, al-Rāzī, al-Nasafī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Biqāʿī, al-Bursawī, and al-Ālūsī argue that created, owned servants cannot be divine offspring."}, {"id": "21:26/q06/p2", "position": "A narrow metaphorical or symbolic title 'Father' can be applied to God, without implying begotten or exclusive divine offspring.", "reasons": "Study Quran reports some Muslim theologians permitting this narrow usage, citing 2:116; those theologians reject superior ontological status from begetting and exclusive sectarian filiation, citing 5:18: people are created mortals subject to God's forgiveness or punishment."}]}
{"id": "21:26/q07", "question": "What does سُبْحَٰنَهُۥ declare?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "21:26/q07/p1", "position": "It declares God exalted and remote from the claim that He has a child.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā ibn Sallām, al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Qurṭubī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī, al-Kashshāf, al-Ālūsī, and Asad apply the declaration to the offspring claim. Al-Bursawī reports Baḥr al-ʿUlūm's exclamation at attributing child, spouse, or partner to the giver of blessings, and al-Kashf's point that glorification can express astonishment too."}]}
{"id": "21:26/q08", "question": "How is سُبْحَٰنَهُۥ parsed?", "turns_on": "Whether the expression is taken as a noun, an elliptical verbal construction, or an imperative.", "positions": [{"id": "21:26/q08/p1", "position": "It is a verbal noun of glorification or a fixed noun for glorification.", "reasons": "Al-Bursawī gives both analyses, with the verbal noun conveying transcendence or remoteness. Al-Ālūsī also lists both."}, {"id": "21:26/q08/p2", "position": "It is an elliptical 'I glorify Him' or an imperative to glorify Him.", "reasons": "Al-Bursawī supplies the implied verb and imperative analysis; al-Ālūsī also allows an imperative."}]}
{"id": "21:26/q09", "question": "What does بَلْ do to the preceding claim?", "turns_on": "Whether bal can retract a human claim quoted in divine speech, or must only begin a new topic.", "positions": [{"id": "21:26/q09/p1", "position": "It cancels the offspring claim and asserts the correction that they are servants.", "reasons": "Sībawayh illustrates correction with 'I passed a man—a donkey,' grammatical only when the latter replaces the earlier identification; he says the angels have already been mentioned. Al-Zarkashī rejects Ibn Mālik's transition-only rule and cites Qur'anic examples 21:5, 27:66, and 38:8. Al-Itqān says a clause following bal can reject a prior assertion; Ibn ʿĀshūr cites 2:116 for this correction."}, {"id": "21:26/q09/p2", "position": "In the Qur'an, bal only moves to a new point and does not retract a prior assertion.", "reasons": "Al-Zarkashī reports Ibn Mālik's claim and rejects it. Al-Itqān attributes it to al-Basīṭ, Ibn Mālik, and Ibn al-Ḥājib, while Ibn Hishām calls it mistaken. Ibn al-Ḥājib argues cancellation of a true first assertion would imply error. Al-Itqān gives a case where bal shifts from success and prayer to preferring worldly life, and distinguishes bal before a single coordinated word, absent from the Qur'an. Al-Itqān adds that before a single word bal is a coordinating conjunction, with no Qur'anic instance."}]}
{"id": "21:26/q10", "question": "How is بَلْ عِبَادٌ مُّكْرَمُونَ constructed?", "turns_on": "Whether ʿibād is a resumed nominative predicate, a corrective replacement, or a hypothetical accusative object.", "positions": [{"id": "21:26/q10/p1", "position": "ʿIbādun is nominative as the predicate of an omitted 'they,' in a resumed statement.", "reasons": "Sībawayh allows a nominative after bal by a resumed clause with omitted huwa and notes even a new utterance may omit a understood phrase; he says the angels are known from context. Al-Jishumī treats it as a new statement detached from the quotation. Al-Samīn and al-Zarkashī supply hum; Ibn ʿĀshūr likewise supplies the angels as subject."}, {"id": "21:26/q10/p2", "position": "The nominative can function as a corrective replacement after bal; a genitive badal is also grammatically conceivable.", "reasons": "Sībawayh compares raising after the accusative waladan with raising after a genitive, and allows a genitive badal governed by bāʾ in an analogous construction. His 'man—a donkey' example is felicitous as replacement, not predication. He says definiteness does not change constructions with lākin, bal, and lā bal; he contrasts aw's movement from certainty to doubt with am's direct choice and reports Yūnus rejecting a genitive in a parallel 'how [about] a woman' construction."}, {"id": "21:26/q10/p3", "position": "A hypothetical accusative ʿibādan would make it the object of 'took': God took honored servants instead of children.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj allows this outside the muṣḥaf but prefers the written nominative. Al-Naḥḥās reports Abū Isḥāq's equivalent wording and al-Farrāʾ's coordination with walad; al-Qurṭubī repeats both analyses. This is presented as a grammatical possibility, not the transmitted reading."}]}
{"id": "21:26/q11", "question": "Whom does عِبَادٌۭ مُّكْرَمُونَ name?", "turns_on": "Whether the corrective plural follows the angel claim specifically or covers the wider claims about Jesus and Ezra.", "positions": [{"id": "21:26/q11/p1", "position": "The phrase names the angels.", "reasons": "Muqātil and most commentators identify angels as the servants denied to be offspring. Al-Zajjāj transmits this as the tafsir view; Abu Ḥayyān reports al-Zamakhsharī's narrower reading. Al-Ṭabarṣī and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī use the context of alleged angelic daughters; Sībawayh says they are already mentioned. Ibn Isḥāq and al-Thaʿlabī add their obedience in speech and action."}, {"id": "21:26/q11/p2", "position": "The phrase names the angels and Jesus son of Mary.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj states this view; al-Naḥḥās reports Abū Isḥāq with the same identification."}, {"id": "21:26/q11/p3", "position": "The phrase includes angels, Jesus, and Ezra.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya reads the verse as rejecting all three groups' filiation claims; Abu Ḥayyān says the phrase can include all three while reporting al-Zamakhsharī's angels-only interpretation."}]}
{"id": "21:26/q12", "question": "What makes these servants مُّكْرَمُونَ?", "turns_on": "Whether honor is described as God's favor and nearness, complete servitude, or protection from error; the notes do not make these mutually exclusive.", "positions": [{"id": "21:26/q12/p1", "position": "God honors, favors, selects, and brings them near.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī glosses ikrām as honoring or showing esteem. Ibn ʿAbbās, reported by al-Wāḥidī, says God honored and selected the angels; Ibn al-Jawzī and al-Ṭabrisī echo selection. Al-Nasafī, Ibn Kathīr, Ibn ʿĀshūr, and al-Ālūsī specify exalted rank or nearness. Al-Kashshāf, Abu Ḥayyān, and al-Ālūsī say their nearness helped provoke the false child claim. Al-Bursawī says preferred over many, not all."}, {"id": "21:26/q12/p2", "position": "Their honor is worship and perfect, bestowed servitude.", "reasons": "Muqātil says God honored them through worship. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls complete servitude God's gift: angels know themselves only as servants, obey perfectly, and lack contrary traits. He contrasts angelic servitude with acquired human servitude and compares mukhliṣ with mukhlaṣ; honor is bestowed on both humans and angels."}, {"id": "21:26/q12/p3", "position": "Their honor includes protection from error or sin.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī identifies the honor as protection from error; al-Jishumī calls angels accountable yet protected from sin, grounding it in their doing what they are commanded."}]}
{"id": "21:26/q13", "question": "How is مُّكْرَمُونَ read?", "turns_on": "Whether the rāʾ is light or geminated.", "positions": [{"id": "21:26/q13/p1", "position": "The common reading has mukramūn without doubling the rāʾ.", "reasons": "Abu Ḥayyān and al-Samīn contrast the majority reading with ʿIkrima's doubled reading; al-Kashshāf also mentions a reading as mukramūn."}, {"id": "21:26/q13/p2", "position": "ʿIkrima reads mukarramūn with a doubled rāʾ.", "reasons

": "Abu Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī attribute it to ʿIkrima. Al-Samīn contrasts it with the general reading; al-Bayḍāwī also reports the doubled consonant."}]}
{"id": "21:26/q14", "question": "What follows from the angels' being honored servants?", "turns_on": "Whether the consequence stressed is obedience and dependence, or their accountability and preservation.", "positions": [{"id": "21:26/q14/p1", "position": "They obey God in speech and deed and cannot act as independent intercessors or objects of worship.", "reasons": "Ibn Isḥāq and al-Thaʿlabī say they do not speak ahead of God and act only by His command. Ibn Kathīr says obedience in word and deed is complete; Kuran Yolu cites 4:172 and includes Jesus' recognition of God's knowledge, power, and majesty. Al-Jishumī says worshipping angels is unwarranted because they worship God. Iṣlāḥī denies autonomous intercession, says they speak only with permission, and warns that claiming partnership ends in Hell. Al-Qurṭubī and Study Quran report Khuzāʿa worshipped them in hope of intercession."}, {"id": "21:26/q14/p2", "position": "They are morally accountable yet preserved from sin.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī infers accountability and protection from the statement that they do what God commands; al-Biqāʿī calls protection from error their honor."}]}
{"id": "21:26/q15", "question": "How does this verse fit the passage's argument?", "turns_on": "Which part of the passage's wider argument the note emphasizes.", "positions": [{"id": "21:26/q15/p1", "position": "After refuting divine partners, the passage turns to the false claim of divine offspring.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says the preceding proof rules out partner, opposite, and rival; Ibn ʿĀshūr says the passage moves from worship of other gods to this belief. Ibn ʿAṭiyya notes the polytheists still acknowledged God as creator and provider."}, {"id": "21:26/q15/p2", "position": "The passage reinforces the prophets' monotheism and God's wise justice over creation.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī says multiple independent divine wills would make the universe unsustainable and all prophets taught monotheism. He also says the universe is no amusement: its just, wise Creator will establish a day when truth defeats falsehood."}]}
{"id": "21:26/q16", "question": "What report about Idrīs is transmitted alongside this verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "21:26/q16/p1", "position": "Idrīs preceded Noah, taught monotheism, allowed his people to choose their conduct, and they refused before God destroyed them.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā ibn Sallām transmits this from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr."}]}
{"id": "21:97/q01", "question": "What does 'has drawn near' convey?", "turns_on": "Whether the verb merely equals qaruba or intensifies it, and whose measure of nearness is used.", "positions": [{"id": "21:97/q01/p1", "position": "The form emphasizes a greater or intensified nearness.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān and Biqāʿī read iftaʿala as intensified; Biqāʿī compares the Hour to a woman about to give birth and cites a hadith. Ālūsī records this alternative."}, {"id": "21:97/q01/p2", "position": "The event has come near, with no distinct force beyond qaruba.", "reasons": "Jishumī equates qaruba and iqtaraba; Ālūsī reports this plain gloss."}, {"id": "21:97/q01/p3", "position": "It is near by God's measure despite people's sense that Judgment is remote.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī contrasts brief human measures with God's measure and cites 70:6–7."}]}
{"id": "21:97/q02", "question": "What is the true promise that approaches?", "turns_on": "Whether waʿd names the final Resurrection, its second trumpet blast, or the individual's death.", "positions": [{"id": "21:97/q02/p1", "position": "The Resurrection or Hour, including the ensuing reckoning and recompense.", "reasons": "Muqātil stresses its certainty; Ṭabarī resurrection from graves for reward and punishment; Bursevī and Ālūsī place resurrection, reckoning, and recompense after the second blast, not the first. Rāzī calls it unquestionable; Ibn ʿĀshūr treats these events collectively. Rāzī calls waʿd a figurative name for the appointed event. Ibn Kathīr links its imminence to terrors and upheavals; Kuranyolu to Gog and Magog as a sign."}, {"id": "21:97/q02/p2", "position": "Specifically the second blast of the Trumpet.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā ibn Sallām identifies the approaching promise with that blast."}, {"id": "21:97/q02/p3", "position": "The minor resurrection at each person's death.", "reasons": "Qāshānī reads the veiled person's horrified stare and admission as occurring at death."}]}
{"id": "21:97/q03", "question": "What does 'true' contribute and what senses of its root are given?", "turns_on": "The notes distinguish this sense from other attested uses of the root.", "positions": [{"id": "21:97/q03/p1", "position": "It is sound, correct, and certain, the opposite of falsehood.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī gives ḥaqq as sound/correct, ḥaqīqa as a matter's true outcome, and ḥaqqa as becoming due; Biqāʿī says the promised event matches what will happen. Ibn al-Jawzī lists ḥāqqa for rival truth-claims, ḥaqqahu/aḥaqqahu for prevailing, and iḥtaqqū for mutual claims."}, {"id": "21:97/q03/p2", "position": "The root also names the all-befalling Resurrection and several concrete things.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī records al-ḥāqqa for Resurrection, ḥiqqa for a rideable young camel and ḥuqāq its plural, ḥuqqa/ḥuqaq for a box, and ḥaqḥaqa for exhausting travel; Muṭarrif's poem contrasts that pace with moderation."}]}
{"id": "21:97/q04", "question": "How does the preceding 'until' introduce this scene?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "21:97/q04/p1", "position": "It links the statements and advances to a new purpose, without requiring a literal temporal endpoint.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr compares Labīd's Muʿallaqah and 2:214, where ḥattā introduces speech arising from distress rather than the endpoint when the Messenger spoke."}]}

{"id": "21:97/q11", "question": "Why retain the pronoun before naming the disbelievers' eyes?", "turns_on": "The notes give both suspense and particularization as effects of the pronoun.", "positions": [{"id": "21:97/q11/p1", "position": "It gives suspense and then clarifies the important scene.", "reasons": "Itqān says the affair-pronoun first leaves the matter vague and then explains it, magnifying the following information; Ibn ʿĀshūr likewise sees advance notice resolved by the following words."}, {"id": "21:97/q11/p2", "position": "It singles out disbelievers as those whose eyes are fixed.", "reasons": "Zarkashī says dropping hiya would lose this particularizing force."}]}
{"id": "21:97/q12", "question": "What does 'staring' mean as a word?", "turns_on": "The physical root senses explain the figurative description of an eye fixed outward.", "positions": [{"id": "21:97/q12/p1", "position": "The eyes are fixed open toward an object, without blinking.", "reasons": "Jishumī lists a gaze fixed outward among the root's senses; Ṭabrisī explains it as if the eye travels toward the object; Abū Ḥayyān, Ibn ʿĀshūr and Rāghib define an immobile, unblinking gaze, often signaling sudden evil or intense attention."}, {"id": "21:97/q12/p2", "position": "The root also describes traveling, displacement, disturbance, or an arrow overshooting.", "reasons": "Jishumī lists a departing traveler, movement between towns, a troubling event, and an arrow passing over its target; Ṭabrisī records travel from home or city as the source image."}]}
{"id": "21:97/q13", "question": "What makes the disbelievers' eyes stare, and where do they look?", "turns_on": "Whether the gaze is specified by its cause, Resurrection's terror, or by its direction toward the caller.", "positions": [{"id": "21:97/q13/p1", "position": "Terror at the Resurrection fixes their open eyes, scarcely blinking.", "reasons": "Muqātil says they see wonders denied in life; al-Kalbī, commentators, Rāzī, Nasafī, Bursevī and Ālūsī describe horror, raised lids and shock. {"id": "21:97/q14", "question": "How is the final tāʾ of 'staring' read when pausing?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "21:97/q14/p1", "position": "In this ṣād-class word the preferred pause uses fatḥ rather than imāla.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī lists ten letters: ḥāʾ, ʿayn, alif and seven emphatics. {"id": "22:5/q04", "question": "What aspect of resurrection is doubted?", "turns_on": "Possibility or actual occurrence.", "positions": [{"id": "22:5/q04/p1", "position": "Whether reviving the dead is possible and within divine power.", "reasons": "Bayḍāwī and Ālūsī emphasize possibility because the following creation proofs show capacity; Ālūsī cites 22:7 for occurrence."}, {"id": "22:5/q04/p2", "position": "Whether resurrection will in fact occur.", "reasons": "Bursevī notes this alternative; Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls it return to God; Islāḥī explains idolaters' reluctance to face accountability."}]}

ed you' answer the condition?", "turns_on": "Whether the clause itself is the answer or evidence for an omitted answer.", "positions": [{"id": "22:5/q06/p1", "position": "Creation is evidence for an implicit command to consider one's origin and recognize resurrection.", "reasons": "Bursevī and Ibn ʿĀshūr note that creation preceded the hearers' doubt, so the literal act of creation cannot be a consequent event; Ālūsī permits the clause to occupy the answer's place."}, {"id": "22:5/q06/p2", "position": "The creation clause directly presents the proof that resolves the conditional doubt.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī and others present the staged first creation as the immediate argument; the one who originated life can restore it."}]}
{"id": "22:5/q07", "question": "How were humans created from dust?", "turns_on": "Whether dust refers to Adam's origin or to the food-chain origin of every human.", "positions": [{"id": "22:5/q07/p1", "position": "It refers to Adam, ancestor of humankind, with descendants included through him.", "reasons": "Zajjāj, Ṭabarī and most commentators name Adam; Rāzī cites 3:59 and 20:55; Ibn ʿĀshūr includes Eve and later reproductive descent; Ālūsī prefers this."}, {"id": "22:5/q07/p2", "position": "Each person derives from earth through nourishment, which becomes reproductive fluid and bodily matter.", "reasons": "Rāzī traces semen and menstrual blood through food to plants, earth and water; Bayḍāwī and Abū Ḥayyān give the same route; Study Quran includes animals and milk."}, {"id": "22:5/q07/p3", "position": "Dust signals humanity's lowly biological kinship with earthy substances.", "reasons": "Asad cites 3:59 and 23:12; Muqātil recalls that humans began as nothing."}]}
{"id": "22:5/q08", "question": "What is a nutfah here?", "turns_on": "Whether the fluid is semen, Adam's own semen, or a fertilized ovum; its base water sense varies.", "positions": [{"id": "22:5/q08/p1", "position": "Semen from which Adam's descendants develop, literally a drop or quantity of water.", "reasons": "Thaʿlabī, Wāḥidī, Qurṭubī and Ālūsī discuss dripping, flowing, or pouring roots; Ṭabrisī includes male and female fluid; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says water may be little or much."}, {"id": "22:5/q08/p2", "position": "Adam's own semen is the intended drop.", "reasons": "Al-Naqqāsh is quoted by Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān; Ālūsī calls this remote."}, {"id": "22:5/q08/p3", "position": "It may name the sperm or the fertilized ovum produced from it.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu uses embryonic context; Elmalılı speaks more precisely of the seed within semen."}]}
{"id": "22:5/q09", "question": "What is an ʿalaqah?", "turns_on": "Whether the word describes congealed blood or an attached early embryo.", "positions": [{"id": "22:5/q09/p1", "position": "A piece of fresh, thick, congealed or clotted blood.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayd emphasizes intense redness; Wāḥidī cites al-Qaṭāmī; al-Samīn cites an Arabic saying about battlefield blood; commentators describe the preceding fluid thickening."}, {"id": "22:5/q09/p2", "position": "It denotes a moist, clinging or attached early stage.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī derives it from adhesion; Islāḥī allows a living leech-like referent; Kur'an Yolu prefers a fertilized ovum attached to the uterine wall."}]}
{"id": "22:5/q10", "question": "What is a muḍghah?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "22:5/q10/p1", "position": "A small piece of flesh about the size of a mouthful to chew.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba compares names for scooped or eaten quantities; Ibn ʿĀshūr explains its morphology; a hadith calls the heart a muḍghah."}]}
{"id": "22:5/q11", "question": "What distinguishes formed from unformed?", "turns_on": "Whether the contrast concerns form, completeness, ensoulment, miscarriage, term birth, or the primordial covenant.", "positions": [{"id": "22:5/q11/p1", "position": "One embryo is visibly shaped, complete or smooth; the other is not yet or imperfectly shaped.", "reasons": "Qatāda's complete/incomplete gloss is widespread. Zajjāj, Rāzī, Zamakhsharī, and Nasafī allow deficiencies in limbs and faculties; Rāzī prefers this because the address concerns future humans."}, {"id": "22:5/q11/p2", "position": "The formed pregnancy lives or reaches birth; the unformed one miscarries before completion.", "reasons": "Mujāhid sometimes describes formed and unformed miscarriages; Ibn Masʿūd's angel report has an unformed drop expelled as blood. Ṭabarī prefers expulsion before completed shaping and ensoulment."}, {"id": "22:5/q11/p3", "position": "The formed receives a spirit; the unformed lacks ensoulment.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī prefers this explanation, and Ibn ʿAbbās links it to life and the widow's waiting period; Bursevī reports an inward version in which unformed is an image without soul."}, {"id": "22:5/q11/p4", "position": "The formed has the primordial covenant; the unformed does not.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās in ʿAṭāʾ's transmission and a report from Abū Jaʿfar identify formed particles in Adam's loins under the covenant; the latter includes expelled semen and pre-ensoulment miscarriage among unformed."}, {"id": "22:5/q11/p5", "position": "Every developmental stage is created and may count as mukhallaqah.", "reasons": "Ibn al-ʿArabī reasons from the root; Qurṭubī prefers repeated creation and cites 23:14, against a sense restricted to an imaged fetus."}]}
{"id": "22:5/q12", "question": "How are the adjectives 'formed and unformed' construed or read?", "turns_on": "Whether they are genitive adjectives or accusative circumstantial expressions.", "positions": [{"id": "22:5/q12/p1", "position": "The common genitive forms modify muḍghah.", "reasons": "Bursevī and Ālūsī make the attachment explicit; al-Samīn identifies the general reading."}, {"id": "22:5/q12/p2", "position": "Accusative forms are read as circumstantial or detached qualifiers.", "reasons": "Al-Kisāʾī permits them; Ibn Abī ʿAblah reads both accusative; Sībawayh allows a circumstantial qualifier even after an indefinite noun, though rare."}]}
{"id": "22:5/q13", "question": "What do reports say about fetal stages and angelic decrees?", "turns_on": "The reports differ on the timing of shaping and angelic writing.", "positions": [{"id": "22:5/q13/p1", "position": "A drop, clot, and morsel each last forty days, followed by ensoulment and decrees.", "reasons": "Ibn Masʿūd's Prophetic report lists provision, life, deeds, and fortune; Qurṭubī derives four months and links it to the widow's waiting period. Ibn Kathīr transmits Ṣaḥīḥayn versions."}, {"id": "22:5/q13/p2", "position": "An angel shapes or records the embryo after roughly forty to forty-five nights.", "reasons": "Abū Dharr and Ḥudhayfa versions mention sex and fortune or bodily features; Ibn Kathīr cites Muslim. Bursevī says an early reference to form means its decree, with visible form later."}, {"id": "22:5/q13/p3", "position": "A settled drop is classified as formed or expelled, and the formed child's particulars are copied from the Mother Book.", "reasons": "Ibn Masʿūd and related reports list sex, provision, lifespan, deeds, fortune, and sometimes burial place; Ṭabāṭabāʾ reconciles changeable and unchangeable tablets."}]}
{"id": "22:5/q14", "question": "What does 'so that We may make clear to you' disclose?", "turns_on": "Whether its object is creation, power, resurrection, guidance, or intentionally left open.", "positions": [{"id": "22:5/q14/p1", "position": "The successive stages and manner of creation in wombs.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā, Ibn Qutayba, Wāḥidī's Ibn Muslim, and Qatāda focus on explaining the stages of human creation. Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports that incomplete embryos and miscarriages make womb stages clear."}, {"id": "22:5/q14/p2", "position": "God's power, wisdom, and choice in creating varied forms.", "reasons": "Naḥḥās and Qurṭubī say the stages display divine power; Biqāʿī argues variation defeats nature as a sufficient cause; Rāzī and Elmalılı add God's free choice."}, {"id": "22:5/q14/p3", "position": "The truth or possibility of resurrection.", "reasons": "The author of al-Naẓm and Bursevī read the stages as disclosure of resurrection; Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls the clause parenthetical; Kur'an Yolu prefers gradual development as the fit with the passage."}, {"id": "22:5/q14/p4", "position": "What people should do, avoid, and practice in worship.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās gives this gloss; Zajjāj connects human creation with guidance and right conduct."}, {"id": "22:5/q14/p5", "position": "The object is omitted to suggest knowledge and signs beyond enumeration.", "reasons": "Zamakhsharī, Bayḍāwī, Biqāʿī, and Ālūsī emphasize breadth; Ālūsī prefers this over restricting the object to resurrection."}]}
{"id": "22:5/q15", "question": "How is لنبين read?", "turns_on": "First-person nūn or third-person yāʾ.", "positions": [{"id": "22:5/q15/p1", "position": "The common reading uses nūn: 'so that We make clear.'", "reasons": "Rāzī and later grammarians contrast this with third-person variants."}, {"id": "22:5/q15/p2", "position": "Ibn Abī ʿAblah and others read with yāʾ: 'so that He make clear.'", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī also names Abū ʿImrān al-Jawnī; Ālūsī calls it a shift in grammatical person."}]}
